did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm’s title dedicates it to the chief musician and the Korahites, and includes the term “alamoth,” traditionally understood as referring to a musical instrument or melody.
Did you know? The psalm describes God with three reassuring terms: “refuge,” “strength,” and “a very present help in trouble”—help that is readily available in times of distress.
Did you know? The psalm portrays faith as standing without fear even in extreme circumstances: the earth changes, and the mountains shake into the heart of the seas.

Did you know? The description of the raging sea and trembling mountains emphasizes the power of nature, yet even within this threatening scene appears the word “Selah,” probably marking a pause or emphasis.
Did you know? In contrast to the raging waters at the beginning of the psalm, a river now appears whose streams gladden the “city of God”—an image of life, joy, and stability.
Did you know? The city’s stability is explained by God’s presence within it: “God is in her midst; she will not be moved.” His help is described as renewed at the break of dawn.
Did you know? The psalm contrasts human turmoil—the nations in uproar and kingdoms tottering—with the voice of God, at which the earth melts.
Did you know? This verse contains a repeated refrain emphasizing security: “The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our stronghold.”
Did you know? The psalm invites its hearers to behold the works of the LORD, especially his power to end wars and break bows, spears, and chariots.
Did you know? The conclusion calls people to cease their struggle and recognize that God is exalted among the nations and throughout the earth.
